Paper: Platonov et al., A Critical Look at the Evaluation of GNNs under Heterophily: Are We Really Making Progress?
Claim_and_evidence: Claim: many popular heterophily benchmarks (esp. Chameleon/Squirrel) are flawed (duplicate nodes → train-test leakage), and on cleaner heterophilous graphs strong simple models and standard GNNs often beat specialized heterophily GNNs. Evidence: duplicate analysis; revised/new heterophilous datasets (e.g. Roman-empire); systematic comparison of MLP/GBDT-style baselines vs GNN variants.
Limitation: Results depend on chosen datasets and splits; removing duplicates changes rankings a lot, so older Chameleon/Squirrel numbers are not trustworthy; not focused on controlled edge-noise stress tests.
Project_use: ANCHOR PAPER. Defines similar vs mixed (homo/hetero) setup; justifies Cora/PubMed + Roman-empire (and filtered Chameleon if used); supports hypothesis that tabular models can beat GNNs on mixed graphs.

Paper: Huang et al., Combining Label Propagation and Simple Models out-performs Graph Neural Networks (Correct & Smooth)
Claim_and_evidence: Claim: for many transductive node-classification benchmarks, a shallow feature-only predictor + Correct & Smooth label-propagation post-processing matches or beats heavy GNNs with far fewer parameters and much less training time. Evidence: comparisons on Planetoid/OGB-style node classification; ablations of Correct vs Smooth steps.
Limitation: Strongest in transductive settings with label correlation on edges; gains shrink if the graph/label structure is weak or noisy; not a full substitute for representation learning in all tasks.
Project_use: Strong non-GNN comparator: MLP/XGBoost (+ optional C&S) vs GCN/GAT/GraphSAGE. Supports the project claim that graph use must be justified, not assumed.

Paper: Kipf & Welling, Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks
Claim_and_evidence: Claim: a simplified spectral graph convolution (GCN) effectively combines node features and neighborhood structure for semi-supervised node classification. Evidence: strong accuracy on Cora/Citeseer/Pubmed with a shallow GCN vs earlier baselines.
Limitation: Assumes useful neighborhood aggregation (works best under homophily); can over-smooth when deep; sensitive to graph quality because every layer mixes neighbor features.
Project_use: Primary graph model for Experiment A (edge dropping). On clean similar graphs GCN should win; as real edges are removed, GCN should approach feature-only baselines.

Paper: Veličković et al., Graph Attention Networks
Claim_and_evidence: Claim: attention over neighbors (GAT) can learn which edges matter and improve node classification vs uniform neighborhood averaging. Evidence: competitive/better results on citation and other node-classification benchmarks vs GCN-style aggregation.
Limitation: Attention does not guarantee robustness to many random/fake edges; extra parameters and tuning cost; still message-passing, so noisy topology can still hurt.
Project_use: Second GNN for comparison. Test whether learned edge weights help under edge deletion (A) or resist fake edges better than GCN (optional extension of B).

Paper: Hamilton et al., Inductive Representation Learning on Large Graphs (GraphSAGE)
Claim_and_evidence: Claim: sampling and aggregating neighbor features (mean/LSTM/pool) learns inductive node embeddings that generalize beyond a single fixed graph. Evidence: large-graph / inductive experiments showing gains over purely transductive baselines.
Limitation: Performance still depends on neighbor signal quality; sampling adds variance; mean aggregation behaves similarly to GCN-style smoothing under noise.
Project_use: Main GNN for Experiment B (fake edges) and similar-vs-mixed comparison. Separates self features from neighbor aggregation — useful when diagnosing when neighbor mixing starts to hurt.

Paper: Zhu et al., Beyond Homophily in Graph Neural Networks: Current Limitations and Effective Designs
Claim_and_evidence: Claim: standard GNNs can fail under heterophily because neighborhood aggregation mixes different-class nodes; designs that better separate ego/neighbor information or use higher-order/compatible neighborhoods help. Evidence: synthetic and real heterophilous benchmarks; analysis of when homophily assumptions break.
Limitation: Some proposed fixes are architecture-specific; dataset choices in early heterophily work were later criticized (see Platonov); does not study random edge injection as a controlled noise protocol.
Project_use: Theory/motivation for Hypothesis 2 (mixed graphs) and for interpreting fake-edge noise as destroying effective homophily. Guides what failure modes to expect when GNN < MLP/XGBoost.
